items.title: Wooden Chappal
items.description: These wooden chappals were traditionally worn by the Gujjar Bakarwals during their daily work and while travelling through forests and mountain trails. Made from wood with straps woven from natural grass fibres, they were strong, comfortable, and easy to make using materials available in nature. The thick wooden sole protected their feet from mud, stones, and damp ground, making them well suited to their nomadic lifestyle.

items.title: Traditional Snow Broom
items.description: This broom was made from mountain grass and attached to a sturdy wooden handle. It was mainly used to remove snow from the roofs of houses during the winter season. Its wide shape made it easier to clear large amounts of snow without damaging the roof. Apart from snow removal, it was also used for cleaning open spaces around the house, making it an important household tool.

items.title: Traditional Mud House
items.description: The Gujjar Bakarwals built their homes using mud, clay, and other natural materials found nearby. The thick mud walls acted as natural insulation, keeping the house warm during the cold winters and cool in the summer months. These homes were simple, affordable, and environmentally friendly, reflecting the community's close relationship with nature and their practical knowledge of local building techniques.

items.title: Wooden Table
items.description: This small wooden table was used for many everyday household activities. It served as a platform for keeping food, utensils, and cooking vessels, and was also used while eating meals. Since families usually sat on the floor, the table was built low to the ground for convenience. Its sturdy design and handmade craftsmanship show how the Gujjar Bakarwals created useful furniture from locally available wood.

items.title: Traditional Mud Stove
items.description: This traditional stove was made from mud and clay and was used for preparing daily meals. It burned firewood, which was easily available in the surrounding forests. The mud structure helped retain heat, making cooking more efficient while using less fuel. It was an essential part of every household, where families prepared bread, milk, tea, and other traditional dishes.

items.title: Traditional Wooden & Earthen Utensils
items.description: The Gujjar Bakarwals used wooden and earthen utensils in their everyday life for cooking, serving, and storing food. Earthen pots kept water and food naturally cool, while wooden bowls and cups were lightweight and durable enough to be carried during seasonal migrations. These utensils reflect the community's simple lifestyle and their use of natural, locally available materials.

items.title: Herbal Medicine Writing Tablet
items.description: This wooden tablet was used to write down information about medicinal plants and traditional remedies. The Gujjar Bakarwals had extensive knowledge of herbs found in the forests and mountains, which they used to treat common illnesses. Recording this knowledge on wooden tablets helped preserve it and allowed it to be passed on from one generation to the next.

items.title: Traditional Butter Churning Pot
items.description: This large earthen vessel was used to churn curd or milk into butter and buttermilk. A wooden churner was placed through the opening and turned by hand until the butter separated from the milk. Since the Gujjar Bakarwals depended heavily on livestock, dairy products formed an important part of their daily diet and livelihood. This vessel represents the importance of milk processing in their traditional way of life.

items.title: Traditional Silver Jewellery
items.description: Silver jewellery was an important part of the Gujjar Bakarwal community's traditional attire. Women wore silver necklaces, earrings, bangles, anklets, and ornaments during festivals, weddings, and other special occasions. Besides enhancing their appearance, these ornaments symbolized cultural identity, family heritage, and social status. The jewellery was handcrafted by local artisans.

items.title: Traditional Colourful Bead Jewellery
items.description: Colourful bead jewellery was commonly worn by Gujjar Bakarwal women as part of their everyday dress. Made from brightly coloured glass beads, seeds, or other locally available materials, these necklaces and ornaments added beauty to their traditional clothing. Easy to make and lightweight, bead jewellery reflected the community's creativity and love for vibrant colours while preserving their rich cultural traditions.
